title: Fire hazard associated with different types of photovoltaic power plants: Effect of vegetation management
abstract:
Synanthropic vegetation occurs at sites of photovoltaic power plants, where vegetation management is typically ignored, and can have adverse effects on photovoltaic panels as they increase fire hazards. Most scientific papers
related to the installation and operation of solar power plants do not address the impact of photovoltaic power plants on vegetation and the associated fire hazards; grasslands, where photovoltaic power plants are usually
located, have abundant grass that is highly flammable. This study was conducted in the South Moravian region of the Czech Republic to monitor and quantify the occurrence of plant species at sites where two different types of
photovoltaic panels were installed. It was hypothesized that different types of photovoltaic panels are associated with different types of vegetation. Vegetation was assessed using phytocoenological relev´es. The vegetation was controlled by grazing sheep and mowing around photovoltaic panels. The results of this study indicated that stationary photovoltaic panels create favourable conditions for species that increase fire hazards. Fire hazards can be reduced using grazing or mowing and removal of biomass. Using rotating photovoltaic panels, combined with sheep grazing, is more effective for promoting vegetation that reduces the chances of fire. This study highlights that photovoltaic power plants represent a renewable and sustainable energy source; however, different types of photovoltaic panels are associated with different vegetation types. To eliminate fire hazards, it is necessary to employ suitable methods of vegetation management (e.g., grazing by animals). Furthermore, combining an appropriate method of vegetation management with rotating photovoltaic panels will further reduce fire hazards.

## **1. Introduction**

The technosphere (i.e., human culture of technological activity) draws a major part of its energy supply from fossil fuels, which are consumed at a rate several times higher than that of their creation. Therefore, the introduction of modern renewable energy technologies is crucial for the current energy transformation [1]. Under the European Green Deal 2020 [2], the new European Commission for 2019–2024

declared its targets of increasing the European Union’s (EU’s) greenhouse gas emissions reduction target to at least 55% (compared to 1990 levels) by 2030, and total climate neutrality by 2050 [3,4]. Solar energy (SE) is a promising alternative energy source to overcome the energy scarcity problem facing humanity, providing heat, light, and/or electricity [3,5,6]. Currently, the most common device used to transform energy from solar radiation into electric energy is a photovoltaic (PV) panel [7]. Since it is difficult to harmonize the conflict between reducing the use of conventional energy sources (such as crude oil and coal) and

increasing energy demand [4,8], the development of PV systems is supported globally [6,9]. According to the World Energy Outlook released by the International Energy Agency (IEA) [10], a major instruments to curb the upward trend of CO2 emissions is to scale-down coal power plants, and create new sustainable structures. The coming decade is expected to see continued growth in renewables. Therefore, solar PV systems and wind technologies will allow the renewable energy market [4,8] to overtake fossil-based sources [11–14]. SE has obvious environmental advantages over other energy sources and will not be depleted (as it is an infinite resource). It does not produce CO2 emissions at the point of electricity production [15–17], since there is a carbon cost associated with the other stages of its life cycle. Currently, many countries have been forced to switch to SE or other alternative sources of energy [18], even though their environmental impacts are still not fully determined [19].

Although one of the main benefits of PV technology is reduced emissions, both economic profit and environmental impacts must be considered during their design [20]. The potential environmental effects associated with SE include land use and habitat loss [21,22], water consumption, other chemicals to clean the modules [23], and the use of hazardous materials in production [24], which can vary greatly, depending on the technology used and installation location. On the sites of photovoltaic power plants (PVPP) with limited focus on vegetation in the context of land management activities, synanthropic vegetation occurs [25] which can increase fire hazard at PVPP sites. According to Hardy [26], fire hazard assessment is based on physical fuel characteristics, such as fuel arrangement, fuel load, condition of herbaceous vegetation, and presence of elevated fuel. Fire risk management in PVPP areas is a component of several factors depending on the method of managing plant biomass. Simultaneously, the presence of grass species favours in these areas with a calorific value exceeding 17,000 MJ.kg[−][1 ] the possibility of rapid fire development. Therefore, mature herbaceous vegetation on PVPP demonstrates a fire positive feedback loop.

Moreover, unmanaged PVPP areas can also become a significant source of weeds, spreading to adjacent land where cultural crops are often grown [25]. However, vegetation on PVPP sites has some positive characteristics— it can be used as fodder for animals, contributes to supporting biodiversity, protects against water and wind erosion [25, 27–29], is a source of nectar and pollen for pollinators [28,30], creates hiding places for fauna, and contributes to the nutrient cycle. Since PV farms are built on land with optimal sunlight, however, this vegetation also increases the risk of hazards, such as fires.

The territorial and landscape effects of PVPP have been widely investigated [31–33]. However, studies on the impacts of PV panels on vegetation characteristics are limited [34–36]. Evidence has shown that although cases are rare, surface fires caused

directly by PV installations are possible [37–39]. The causes of fires at PVPP sites vary and the most common causes include the faulty installation of quick couplers or the selection of incorrect quick couplers, inadequate cable routing, failure to use shields on them, or the use of inadequate adapters, which can lead to electric arc formation that directly causes fires [37,38]. Sometimes, there are design errors, including too many parallel connections, that have affected several installations [39]. Occasionally, fires are caused by animals that damage the installations. This means that fires are started by the panels and then proceed to the soil surface and vice versa. According to Aram et al. [40] there is no effective system recording fire events initiated by the solar panel system.

Therefore, a study was conducted to monitor and quantify the occurrence of plant species (covering production biomass, frequency of occurrence) on a site in the Czech Republic with stationary and rotating PVPP. Goals of the present study are to: (i) study the vegetation composition associated with two different vegetation management practices (grazing and mowing) and two different types of PV panels, stationary and rotating; (ii) identify the plant species that are tolerant to grazing and mowing on the site with PVPP; and (iii) indicate the fire hazard caused by biomass accumulation with different PV panel designs and vegetation management. It was hypothesized that: (i) vegetation composition on a PVPP site will be different between grazing and mowing; and (ii) the design of rotating PV panels allows the control of vegetation and amount of biomass (by creating favourable conditions for the occurrence of clovers and annual herbs), which have a positive effect on reducing the fire hazard. In the present study, an attempt was also made to demonstrate that different vegetation management practices (grazing and mowing) can lead to different outcomes regarding plant species composition and thus alter the impacts of fire hazards.

## **2. Material and methods**

## _2.1. Study site_

The PVPP site occurs on the outskirts of Moravský Krumlov town (South Moravian Region, Czech Republic) (49[◦] 03[′] 12.1[′′] N 16[◦] 17[′] 41.2[′′] E), between Bohemian-Moravian Highland (Ceskomoravsk[ˇ] a  ́ vysoˇcina) and Dyje R.-Svratka R. Graben (Dyjsko-svratecký úval). The primary geological units are formed by the Bohemian Massif in the Northwest and Carpathians in the Southeast. The secondary units of the Bohemian Massif include Moldanubicum, Boskovice Furrow (Boskovick ́a brazda), and Brno Massif. Soils surrounding the town of  ́ Moravský Krumlov are mostly loamy sands and sandy loams with predominant chernozems. Soil-forming substrates are carbonates containing sediments, such as loess loams, sandy loess loams, and marls. This locality is in a warm climatic region with a long-term mean annual temperature of 9.4[◦] C and precipitation of 629.6 mm. The region is characterized by long, warm, and dry summers, very short transition periods, warm springs, and autumns, and dry winters with a very short duration of snow cover. Altitude of the site is 340 m above sea level. Potential natural vegetation is _Carpini-Querceta_ and _Carpini-Querceta Tiliae_ . This property was originally used as farmland.

The PVPP (Fig. 1), established towards late 2009, is a singular solar PVPP that uses automated swivel stands with the polar axis for tracing the sun, extended with ridge radiation concentrators in addition to the traditional stationary PV panels. To increase the yield, double-sided bifacial solar panels were used to generate electric energy both from their front and their back.

The discussed PVPP are different because they relate to various technologies of their supporting construction. The stationary construction is a standard structure commonly used when building PVPP; however, the rotating structure is a _Super TRAXLE_ comb concentrator. Polycrystalline PV panels were installed on the stationary construction, and monocrystalline panels were installed on the rotating construction. The rotating PVPP, with a nominal installed output of 432 kWp, features

an annual production of 650 MWh, generating almost the same amount of energy as the stationary PVPP with the nominal installed output of 650 kWp. The total area of the site is 8.2 ha. In spring 2010, the grass mixture was hand sown at 20 kgha[−][1] . The composition of the grass mixture was 70% _Lolium perenne,_ 25% _Festuca rubra_ , and 5% _Dactylis glomerata_ .

## _2.2. Vegetation survey_

Vegetation was assessed using phytocoenological relev ́es according to the standard principles of the Zürich-Montpellier approach [25]. Data were collected in the field. Plant species were identified on the monitored study site over three months (i.e., July, August, and September) each year in 2013, 2014, and 2015, and their vegetation cover was then quantified. Vegetation management treatments and PVPP site

conditions are schematically presented in Fig. 2.

The vegetation on the site is controlled by the grazing of sheep, which move freely around the PVPP site. Plots where the vegetation was annually mowed at the end of the growing period were fenced to prevent sheep access. In each variant, three relev ́es were recorded, with an area of 3 × 3 m; all relev ́es were recorded at the same place each time. The individual permanent phytocoenological relev ́es were evenly distributed between rows of PV arrays to represent the vegetation composition. The phytocoenological relev ́es areas did not touch each other and were placed in different rows of PV panels. The coverage of detected plant species was estimated directly by percentage (%), and all plant species were measured for maximum stand height (in m). The cover estimation and plant measurements were determined in the area of the phytocoenological relev ́es by the same person throughout the study period. The biomass of individual plant species (i.e., Index of biomass ( _IB_ )) was

calculated using the following equation (Eq. (1)):

_IB_ = _c_ × _hm_ (1)

Where, _c_ (%) is coverage of plant species, and _hm_ (m) is maximum height.

The scientific names of individual plant species used in this study originate from the Pladias database of Czech flora and vegetation [41].

## _2.3. Data processing and statistical analyses_

Evaluation of the vegetation cover and plant height was spatially defined by 8 treatments (Fig. 2): 2 types of PV panels (stationary and rotating) × 2 sampling locations (under and between) × 2 management practices (mowing and grazing). The data set intended for statistical processing has 216 records (8 treatments × 3 replicates × 3 summer sampling periods × 3 years) of _IB_ values from all treatments and all sampling periods. The _IB_ values of individual plant species in the treatments were processed by employing a multidimensional analysis of the ecological data. The first method was Detrended Correspondence Analysis (DCA), which provided the gradient length. DCA is a technique to summarize ecological changes through time and ordinating ecological data. Response data are compositional and have a gradient 3.0 standard deviation (SD) units long, so a linear method is not appropriate. Further statistical evaluation was then conducted using Canonical Correspondence Analysis (CCA), where the time factors (i.e., month and year) were entered into the analysis as a covariate to avoid pseudo replication. This shows the association between the selected factors (PV panel types and vegetation management). Multivariate analyses explain the relationship between the explanatory variables, and relationship between the plant species found. This analysis aimed at determining associations between vegetation composition and the different types of PV panels and vegetation management practices. Statistical significance was further established using the Monte Carlo test, wherein 999 permutations were calculated. _IB_ data were processed using the Canoco 4.0. computer programme [42].

## **3. Results**

Eighty-three plant species were detected during the three years of monitoring at the PVPP site. Table 1 presents the average _IB_ values (%/m) calculated for various plant species groups.

Average _IB_ values of individual species were calculated from values obtained from 3 replicates over 3 years and 3 sampling periods (July, August, and September). Subsequently, the average _IB_ values for individual treatments were calculated.

Fig. 3 shows, in graphical form, the shares of various plant species groups in their respective PVPP treatments. The _IB_ values were similar between PV panel types, being only about 3% higher for stationary PV panels than for rotating PV panels. Significant differences were observed in the _IB_ values for the vegetation management options. The grazing option had _IB_ values approximately 30% lower than the mowing option. _IB_ values were about 7% higher between PV panels compared to under PV panels. The calculated data show that the highest _IB_ values of panels

with higher risk of flare-up (grasses-perennial) were measured for both rotating and stationary plants in mowing mode. All monitored months (July, August, September) in this regime reached 29.45% higher _IB_ values for grasses-perennial than in the grazing regime. Comparing rotary and stationary PV panels in mowing mode, 4.73% higher _IB_ values for grasses-perennial are shown by rotary PV panels. Suitable variants for fire prevention by biomass accumulation appears to be rotating PV panels in grazing mode, regardless of whether it is between or under the PV panels.

_IB_ values of the plant species, as acquired from the monitored experimental treatments during the three years, were initially processed using DCA analysis. The length of the calculated gradient was established by DCA to be 3.97. Based on this calculation, CCA was chosen for further processing. Results of this analysis are graphically expressed using an ordination diagram (Fig. 4).

Based on this analysis, the recorded plant species can be divided into three groups according to the relationship of plant species to the observed factors. In Table 2, the plant species found are assigned to the variants according to the CCA analysis (goal (i) and (ii)). The result of α = 0.001. ## **4. Discussion**

## _4.1. Vegetation structure of the two types of PV panels_

The results of the CCA indicated that PV panels create diverse conditions for plant species (Fig. 4). The species composition in the treatments with stationary PV panels are more alike than those with rotating PV panels, possibly owing to the vertical height of the PV panel from the ground. In the stationary PV panels, the angle of tilt of all panels remains the same, and the height above the ground does not change.

The height of the stationary panels from the ground to the bottom edge of the panel is approximately 0.65 m (Fig. 5a, point A), whereas that from the ground to the upper edge ranges from 2.2 to 2.5 m (Fig. 5a, point B). Therefore, regarding the construction of stationary PV panels, there are no major changes related to insolation or rainwater supply, allowing the conditions of vegetative development to remain consistent throughout the year, creating a relatively stable environment [46,47]. Rotating PV panels are placed higher than stationary panels, and the angle of inclination and height above the ground vary throughout the year. The height of the panels from the ground to the lower edge can vary from 0.7 to 3 m (Fig. 5b, points A1 and A2), whereas the height from the ground to the upper edge can vary from 2 to 7 m (Fig. 5b points B1 and B2). In this case, conditions conducive to the development of various vegetation types, such as insolation or irrigation, may change significantly throughout the year.

Based on the results, referring to goal (i) and (ii), it can be stated that different types of vegetation are associated with different types of PV panels (Table 1). Especially, the group annual grasses and other herbs—perennial is more represented on the variant with stationary PV panels. According to Hudelsona and Liethb [43] shade tolerant crops

The results indicate that stationary PV panels create favourable conditions for the occurrence of perennial herbs (e.g., _Artemisia vulgaris_ )

and annual grasses (e.g., _Bromus sterilis_ , _Hordeum murinum_ ). These are mainly drought-resistant and shade-tolerant species. Shade-tolerant species deter fire through (a) dense shading that promotes moist, cool microclimates, and (b) the production of fuels that are not conducive to burning (flaccid, moisture-holding leaf drop; moist, rapidly decaying debris) [44]. Furthermore, stationary PV panels create both a permanent rain and light shadow. Plants rely on groundwater or water from surrounding areas and have a limited light source; however, some perennial herbs can withstand these conditions, such as _Cichorium intybus_ , _Convolvulus arvensis_ , _Picris hieracioides_ , _Plantago lanceolata_ , _Plantago media_ , _Taraxacum_ sect. _Taraxacum_ from the survey. In contrast, rotating PV panels have no permanent precipitation and light shadow.

According to Marrou et al. [45] and Uldrjan et al. [25], plants are exposed to shading by stationary PV panels, which results in a limited radiation environment being created below the panels. Since the interception of sunlight by PV cells are the basis of the PVPP design, the absence of direct sunlight beneath stationary PV panels is unavoidable. In such installations, only indirect light from around the edges will be available to plants on the ground. This could potentially be an advantage in arid regions, as some shading will benefit plants during peak sunlight hours and provide hospitable conditions for shade-tolerant plants [25, 27]. Nagengast et al. [46] and Jahanfar et al. [47] confirmed that the shading from a PV panel reduced direct solar radiation, which in turn led to reduced drought stress for the plants growing under it. Research results of Uldrijan et al. [25] highlighted that the dominant species between and under stationary PV panels were: _Achillea millefolium, Potentilla anserina_ , and _Plantago major_ , which are species tolerant to shading either by higher grasses or PV panels. Biomass production in species with lower maximum height positively correlates with the microclimate created by shade. The results of the present study confirmed the research results of Uldrjan et al. [25], with similar species occurring under the stationary PV panels. Species with lower maximum height produce less biomass and therefore pose less of a fire hazard. However, groups of annual grasses produce biomass that dries out quickly and accumulates. The biomass of annual grasses has the potential to create conditions suitable for fires. Murphy et al. Rotating PV panels create favourable conditions for the occurrence of clovers (e.g., _Trifolium repens, Melilotus officinalis_ ) and annual herbs (e. g., _Cerastium holosteoides_ ). These are mainly dicotyledonous species, which prefer direct sunlight. This is possibly the result of different lighting conditions. Regarding rotating PV panels, the vegetation is only in shade during the part of the day with the most intense light. During the rest of the day there is no shade formation. The results indicate that there are differences between stationary and rotating PV panels in species composition due to differences in shading between the two technologies.

The dominant plant species in the rotating PV panel area produce biomass that grows more slowly, remains alive for a relatively long time, and is consumed by herbivores. Therefore, biomass of these species poses less fire hazard.

Based on Table 1 and Fig. 3, it is evident that the _IB_ changes throughout the growing season. During the first observation (i.e., July), _IB_ is the lowest recorded in this study; during the second evaluation (i.e. August), it is the highest recorded, and by the end of the growing season (i.e. September), the increase in biomass is already lower. The beginning of the growing season (from the beginning of spring till July) is

characterized by the increasing biomass. During the vegetation season, biomass growth is dependent on sufficient water [49,50]. The vegetation dies and regenerates, thus accumulating biomass (from July till September [51]. This development is natural and corresponds to the course of the vegetation period (from spring to autumn) in the monitored area.

Comparing the structure of vegetation of the two types of PV panels, _IB_ values are not similar for perennial grasses. Stationary PV panels create conditions for higher _IB_ values for annual grasses and perennials, whereas rotating PV panels create conditions for clovers and annual herbs to have higher _IB_ values. From Table 1 and Fig. 3, it is also evident that the vegetation under the PV panels have lower _IB_ values, especially in clovers, perennial, and annual herbs compared to _IB_ values between the PV panels. The lower biomass under PV panels reflects a reduction in microclimatic factors that are positively associated with productivity: lower temperatures and radiation [52]. In contrast, significantly higher _IB_ values were found in annual grasses under the PV panels compared to _IB_ values between the PV panels (Table 1). Thus, different types of vegetation are associated with different types of PV panels.

## _4.2. Vegetation structure depending on vegetation management_

Different PVPP vegetation management techniques result in different plant species compositions. ‘Stationary PV panels limit vegetation management activities under the panels due to restricted space available for mechanised mowers. The limit regulation create the conditions for the occurrence of ruderal plant species, i.e., typical of disturbed and unmanaged sites. Rruderal species that produce tall to medium-tall biomass ( _Arrhenatherum elatius_ , _Artemisia vulgaris_ , _Bromus hordeaceus_ , _Elytrigia repens_ , _Hordeum murinum_ , _Lolium perenne_ , _Medicago sativa_ , _Melilotus officinalis_ ) are associated with the fire hazard. The occurrence of these species on plots with stationary PV panels is also confirmed by Uldrijan el al [25]. The retention of standing dead biomass is one of the most important plant properties involved in flammability [53].

Rotating PV panels and sheep grazing (Group 2) create more favourable conditions for the occurrence of clovers (e.g., _Trifolium repens, T. pratense, T. arvensea_ ) and annual herbs (e.g., _Cerastium holosteoides, Papaver rhoeas_ ). These species often remain relatively short and their potential for biomass production and accumulation is also lower than species at the stationary PV panels. Other species producing larger amounts of biomass in this variant were _Apera spica-venti, Rumex acetosella,_ and _R. crispus_ —plant species that are rarely grazed by livestock. Therefore, these plants can grow undisturbed and increase their biomass, thus the fire hazard is higher.

Treatments with rotating PV panels and mowing (Group 1) were more suitable for the occurrence of perennial grasses (e.g., _Arrhenatherum elatius_ , _Calamagrostis epigejos, Dactylis glomerata_ , _Festuca rubra_ , _Phleum pratense_ ) and herbs (e.g., _Ballota nigra_ , _Echium vulgare_ , _Symphytum officinale_ ). According to goal (iii), this variant creates the most favourable conditions for biomass production (accumulation) and hence has the highest potential for fire hazard, since increased biomass leads to increased flammability.

Comparing the two types of vegetation management, sheep grazing significantly reduces _IB_ , especially in perennial grasses and perennial herbs, whereas limited mowing leads to their increase in _IB_ ; however, clover and annual herbs showed higher _IB_ values under grazing than under mowing. Murphy et al. [48] emphasises that grazing by large herbivores reduces grass biomass and subsequent fire frequencies. Moreover, Freitag et al. [54] conformed that where grassland vegetation is shaped by grazing, fires are suppressed, as grazers preferentially feed on grasses.

## _4.3. Vegetation structure in relation to fire hazard_

According to Keane [55], green biomass (GB) is one of the most interesting fuels due to its biodiversity. The species within this diverse type of fuel vary significantly in terms of phenology, morphology, and life cycle stages, resulting in a wide range of fuel bed conditions throughout the year. Keane [55] confirmed that the study of green fuel via GB is difficult, due to the large number of species included in the fuel layer, as well as changes in the properties of the deposit, i.e., its condition and humidity, both of which change daily and annually. Simultaneously, it should be emphasized that grassy biomass as a fuel is highly flammable, especially during strong winds [56] due to susceptibility to drying, high local densities, and morphological adaptation of grasses to easy ignition. After drying, the blades and leaves of the grasses remain straight, creating loosely packed and layered fuel beds that easily transfer surface fire, further confirmed by Higgins at al [57]. In the study site, species producing grassy biomass were mainly: _Agrostis capillaris_ , _Dactylis glomerata_ , _Lolium perenne_ , and _Poa pratensi._ According to Winkler et al. [58], _Arrhenatherum elatius_ and _P. pratensi_ are particularly important in terms of fire hazard. Most grassland fires have potential for high intensity combustion, mainly in the flame phase; however, these fires are short-lived. In grassy areas, which have accumulated larger deposits of wet or undecomposed GB, smouldering may also occur locally. Marrou et al. [59] confirmed that there are seven main causes

that lead to PVPP-related ignition incidents. One of the main causes of fires is electric discharge. However, quantitative research results show that 33% of fire incidents in photovoltaic cells are caused by unknown or unrelated ignition sources.

Armstrong et al. [52] found that the influence of PVPP can lead to differences in plant diversity and aboveground vegetation [60,61], which creates the necessary preconditions for fires [62,63]. Furthermore, the conditions required for fires are influenced by the climate and state of vegetation. Plant biomass fuel load changes seasonally, or due to annual variability in precipitation, which can curb or support fires spreading [64–68]. The main components of PVPP installations contributing to PVPP fires are connectors, which are responsible for 27% of all such incidents [69]. On a PVPP site, the amount of GB is adequate for a higher hazard of fires since biomass accumulates around the PV panels during the growing season. Therefore, this increases the fire load in the immediate area of the installation. Conditions of limited biomass mowing increase the potential of fire hazards, which is enhanced in dry and warm weather. This situation is currently observed in the Czech Republic [70]. Of the species found in the study site, the biomass of annual grasses ( _Bromus_ sp., _Hordeum murinum_ ) is important for the _Bromus_ ignition of fires. sp. invasion has resulted in increased fire frequency, size, and intensity in parts of the western United States [71]. The biomass of tall perennial grasses ( _Calamagrostis epigejos_ , _Arrhenatherum elatius_ ) also affects fire hazards [58]. The biomass of perennial herbs ( _Artemisia vulgaris_ , _Rumex crispus_ , _Verbascum densiflorum_ ) is important for continued burning. All these factors clearly indicate that continuous biomass control should be sought, thereby maintaining the acceptable fire load of the site on which the PVPP is located.

Some research has shown that sheep grazing significantly reduces the amount of GB and directly affects vegetation structure, in addition to changing the species composition of local vegetation [72,73]. Thus, grazing is an effective method to control vegetation on sites with PVPP. Unfortunately, sheep often browse on the panels (cables), which increases the danger of short circuiting and potential fire. The reduction of above-ground GB can also result in a smaller plant transpiration surface and greater soil exposure to radiation and weather in grazed areas [74]. Other studies reported that grazers may remove foliage and understorey vegetation, leading to increased soil temperature concomitant with decreased soil moisture [74,75]. These changes in soil temperature and moisture regimes may have important consequences for potential fire hazards.

PVPP-related vegetation management should fulfil several functions: first, it must ensure that vegetation does not grow onto and shade the PV panels. This requires certain interventions that increase the cost of operating the PVPP, which is why less-demanding management options are sought. A variant is created to reduce the intensity of mowing, which has a positive effect on biodiversity but increases the biomass, which further increases the potential for fire hazards.

## **5. Conclusions**

The analysis of species composition and biomass index of vegetation occurring on site with PVPP demonstrated that the dominant species are perennial grasses and herbs across the different treatments. Vegetation biomass tends to accumulate during the growing season, i.e., under conditions of limited biomass mowing, and the potential of fire hazards increase in dry and warm weather. Because the species composition changes as the environment changes, we can use species as indicators of the environmental conditions for practical management purposes. Based on the results, different types of PV panels create different conditions for vegetation, resulting in different species compositions. Stationary PV panels create more suitable conditions for the occurrence of annual grasses and some species of perennial herbs, whereas rotating panels create conditions favourable for the occurrence of clovers and annual herbs. Fire hazards can be reduced by grazing or biomass removal. The design of rotating PV panels is favourable for vegetation control,

reducing the amount of biomass accumulation. It is recommended that the amount of precipitation on PVPP in temperate climates be monitored, because low precipitation in the second half of summer and during autumn may lead to an increased fire hazards. The contribution of this research is to highlight that PVPP represent a renewable and sustainable source of energy, possibly resulting in new conditions for local vegetation. PVPP impact solar radiation fluxes (and thus temperature), wind speed, and turbulence (thus the exchange of biogenic gases and water vapour), and the distribution of precipitation within the solar park. PVPP may have cooling or warming effects on surface temperature. The shade may lead to lower temperatures during the day and higher temperatures at night, which affect many important plant–soil processes, including productivity and decomposition. More moisture in the air may also appear, which can have a positive effect on plant biomass. Scientific research has shown contradictory results so far. However, considering accelerating climate change, the sites of PVPP may become a source of increased fire hazards, if not properly managed. To eliminate this risk, it is necessary to use suitable methods of vegetation management, such as grazing animals or regular mowing of vegetation.
